disclosures.question: Source inventory: what actually feeds the morning report, and how do duplicates and corrections arrive?
disclosures.response: Fictional DBA Dev: “The ERP is SQL Server; I will confirm the exact version and whether it is a single instance or an availability group. Inspections live in dbo.Inspection and dbo.InspectionResult, updated in place. A nightly package copies the day's rows into a reporting database at 22:10; if it fails and retries, it re-sends rows it had already delivered, so the reporting database can hold the same inspection twice. Corrections do not touch the ERP: they arrive as a CSV on a file share with the same inspection ID and a higher source revision, and the package appends them as new rows. The plant sheet is pasted from the reporting database and edited afterwards. Sensor events sit in a separate historian and are not part of the report. Change data capture is not enabled and needs a change request. The full inventory is in the data pack.”

disclosures.question: Metric definition: how is the defect rate computed today, and why do the two reports disagree?
disclosures.response: Fictional analyst Sam: “The workbook averages the per-row defect rate, defective divided by inspected, over every row in the reporting extract with a positive inspected quantity, grouped by load date. It does not remove duplicated rows or drop a superseded revision, because the extract has no flag for either. The plant sheet sums units over whatever rows are pasted, including a negative quantity someone typed as an adjustment, and groups by inspection date. On the day we argued about, once I had pasted the correction in by hand, the workbook said 7.1 percent, the sheet said 10.8 percent, and the figure quality later agreed was 5.0 percent. Nobody is lying; the three numbers answer three different questions. When a row comes through with more defects than units, I delete it and move on; there is nowhere to record that.”

disclosures.question: Failure timeline: what happened the night the report was stale?
disclosures.response: Fictional data lead Leo: “The package started at 22:10, the East extract blocked behind a month-end batch, the job failed at 23:05, retried once, re-sent the first North batch, which held inspection A, and failed again on East. The failure email went to a shared mailbox. The dashboard refresh at 01:10 loaded the partial data anyway, so at 07:30 the board said ‘updated 01:10’ with East showing the previous day and inspection A counted twice in North. The corrections file with A version 2 landed at 06:40 and was not picked up until the next night. The meeting sent our one free quality engineer to North Line 1. The East batch with three defects in nine, which was the real problem, was seen the next day. Someone also deleted ‘duplicate’ rows in the reporting database by hand that afternoon; there is no record of which. The full sequence is in the data pack's failure timeline; the times are fictional but the pattern is the one we live with.”

disclosures.question: Operational capacity: who can run and support a new path, and when?
disclosures.response: Fictional data lead Leo: “Two engineers, about four hours a week each for eight weeks, then less. One shared DBA whose change windows are Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Plant IT is staffed 06:00 to 18:00 and nobody is on call overnight. The corrections file is approved on Fridays by quality, sometimes mid-week for an urgent case. The analyst who maintains the workbook is away one week a month and has no backup. Any alert that fires at 23:05 will be read at 06:30 at the earliest, so the design has to assume that.”

disclosures.question: Plant controller: what does the current disagreement cost, and what baseline can be measured?
disclosures.response: Fictional plant controller Priya: “For this exercise only, treat these as hypothetical planning figures, not audited numbers. The analyst spends about six hours a week reconciling the workbook and the sheet, the plant coordinator about an hour a day, and the quality lead about two hours a week chasing corrections: roughly thirteen hours a week in total. A misdirected morning investigation costs about four engineer-hours, and a held shipment adds expediting cost of around $250 per unit affected. We do not log how often the report causes a wrong decision, so any avoided-cost figure needs its own measurement before anyone counts it.”

scenarios.model:
### 1. Discovery synthesis and the decision
The decision is whether a bounded one-plant quality pilot is justified, and the evidence that matters is the disputed morning report, not a platform comparison. I would open with Mara's most recent disagreement: what action changed, which definitions conflicted, when approved data was actually available, and who noticed. "Real time" was never the requirement: the 8 a.m. meeting needs a trusted plant/day figure by 07:30 with an honest freshness statement.

Acceptance roles, proposed until confirmed: Mara accepts operational usefulness; Imani the metric and correction policy; Leo, the DBA and the analyst establish source semantics, feasibility and a baseline; Noor accepts data and network access; Priya owns the baseline effort figures; Elena decides whether evidence and cost justify expansion; an operator must acknowledge alert and replay duties before anyone relies on the feed.

Known within this fiction: three plants; a SQL Server ERP with a nightly ETL whose retries and reruns re-send rows already delivered; corrections as CSV with the same inspection ID and a higher revision; a hand-edited plant sheet; a workbook that averages per-row rates; thirteen hypothetical reconciliation hours a week; two engineers at four hours a week each; no overnight cover. Still unknown: ERP version and topology, CDC permission, classification, AWS region and connectivity, the business-day boundary, the restatement policy, how often the report misdirects a decision, actual prices, and the named operator. Each gap carries an owner and the decision it can change.

The buying decision changes if the team can trust the plant/day metric before the meeting, see when it is stale, and operate the path inside the disclosed capacity. A polished demo does not satisfy that.

### 2. Source semantics
The inventory separates systems of record from derived copies. The ERP tables are the operational record, but they update in place and expose no history, so a corrected inspection overwrites its row. The nightly ETL's reporting table is a derived copy, not a source; the package's extract step is admitted only as the delivery channel for ERP records, and its retries manufacture duplicates: an exact re-send is one event delivered twice, not two inspections. The corrections file is the only approved channel for revisions, and its `source_revision` is the ordering signal Imani named; arrival and row order are not. The plant sheet is a consumer treated as a source; it is refused at admission, so its pasted copies and typed adjustments never enter revision comparison. B's negative quantity is a different case: it arrived through the ERP extract, so it is admitted as delivered and then quarantined by validation. The sensor historian and the manual library are out of scope.

Two consequences follow. Ingestion admits rows only from the approved channels (the nightly extract and the manual rerun for ERP records, the corrections file for revisions) and labels each with its delivery, so a plant-sheet paste cannot masquerade as a revision. And the business day belongs to the inspection, not the load timestamp: the workbook groups by load date, which is why a correction for the 2nd is counted against whichever day it happens to be loaded.

### 3. The metric contract
Grain: one accepted inspection, by `inspection_id`, at its highest valid approved revision. Measure: total defective units over total inspected units of accepted inspections, per plant and business day; never a mean of per-row rates. Denominator: accepted inspections only; quarantined and unapproved rows are excluded and their count disclosed beside the figure. Time: the inspection's business day, plant-local, midnight boundary unless quality specifies a shift boundary. Restatement: an approved higher revision restates the business day it belongs to; the snapshot carries `evidence_as_of` and `snapshot_id` so two readers can tell which version they saw. Freshness: per plant, the newest approved delivery included and whether any is pending. Completeness: a nightly delivery counts only when its package run finishes with a completion marker; until then its rows are retained and nothing from that run is published, while a corrections file is complete on its own. Staleness: when publication is blocked, the last verified snapshot stays visible, labelled stale, with the reason.

Applied to the disputed North day, the three reports answer three questions. The workbook's mean of per-row rates over four positive rows gives (0.100 + 0.100 + 0.083 + 0.000) / 4 = 7.1%. The plant sheet's sums over all five pasted rows, including B's negative quantity, give 4 / 37 = 10.8%. The contract gives accepted A v2 12/1 and C v1 8/0, totals 20/1, 5.0%, with B disclosed as quarantined. Nobody lied; only the third figure answers "what share of inspected units was defective."

### 4. Ingestion, publication and recovery policy
The policy is the preserved reliable-data policy, unchanged, with a source-admission stage and a delivery-completeness check in front. Stages: admit rows from approved deliveries only; retain every raw row with its delivery identity; validate and quarantine (negative or null quantities, defective above inspected, missing key, unusable version); resolve identity and revision; gate publication (complete deliveries only, no unresolved conflict); publish a snapshot; run external effects once per snapshot.

The five-row example is the acceptance test. Rows (ev1, A, v1, 10/1) delivered twice, (ev2, B, v1, −3/1), (ev3, A, v2, 12/1) and (ev4, C, v1, 8/0) resolve to accepted A v2 12/1 and C v1 8/0, B quarantined, totals 20/1, rate 5%. A replay of an already retained event increases raw and audit counts but changes no accepted total and creates no second effect. An older revision, such as a late re-export of A v1, cannot replace v2; it agrees with history and is ignored for current state. A valid approved A v3 14/1 gives 22/1 exactly once, however many times its file is re-sent. Two deliveries claiming the same key and revision with different quantities are a conflict; the gate blocks publication of any new report and the last verified 20/1 snapshot stays published and explicitly stale. On a first run with no verified snapshot, the state is blocked with no snapshot, and 8/0 for C alone is not a publishable report. Nothing in the pipeline adjudicates a conflict; the cure is upstream, at source admission and in quality's approval process, and the gate reads its own decision row rather than inferring safety from an empty unresolved list.

Recovery follows the retained boundaries. Failure after raw retention leaves the previous snapshot explicitly stale; recovery recomputes from retained rows and publishes once. Failure after publication but before the effect leaves a correct report with a pending effect, recorded once against the snapshot identity. Absence from a later incremental delivery is never a deletion. The same rule covers the ETL rerun, the Friday corrections file and a manual re-run at 11:15.

### 5. Stale versus current: what the night cost
The failure timeline shows the difference between explicitly stale and silently wrong. It separates what the logs show from what people inferred, and so does this section.

Facts within the fiction: the package failed at 23:05, and its retry re-sent inspection A before failing again on East. East was missing when the 01:10 refresh loaded the partial day anyway. At 07:30 the board said "updated 01:10", carried no evidence time and counted A twice in North, so the workbook read 6.7% and the sheet 12.0%. The corrections file with A v2 had been on the share since 06:40 and was not picked up until the next night. The 08:00 meeting sent the one available quality engineer to North Line 1. G's East batch, 3 defects in 9 units, reached the meeting a day later. Someone deleted rows by hand at 13:00, and nobody recorded which.

Hypotheses, each needing its own evidence before it enters a design: that a month-end batch caused the East lock (unconfirmed); that North Line 1 had a problem (the meeting's reading of two undated numbers); that East was the real problem the meeting should have investigated (Mara's and Leo's view, which G's figures support but nobody has investigated); and that the 10:40 paste fixed the figure.

Under the contract the same night produces a different screen. D1 closes at 01:10 without a completion marker, so North is held: the board shows the last verified North day labelled stale with the reason, and East labelled "no delivery for 2 March". The corrections delivery is admitted at 06:40, but North stays held until the run completes. At 11:15 the manual rerun completes it: North publishes 20/1 at 5.0% with `evidence_as_of` 11:15, and East publishes 44/5 at 11.4%. Nobody acts on 6.7% or 12.0% at 07:30, or on 7.1% and 10.8% later. Explicit staleness changes the meeting's action: escalate the missing delivery and defer the North judgement rather than act on a number nobody can date.

The business impact uses Priya's hypothetical figures, not a savings claim: about four engineer-hours per misdirected investigation and roughly $250 per unit of expediting on held shipments. Because Cinderline does not log how often the report misdirects a decision, this stays out of the base value case until the incident log supplies a count.

### 6. Two defensible paths
Path A, governed lakehouse: approved deliveries land in an AWS bucket in the customer account; a scheduled job retains raw, validates, resolves and publishes into a Unity Catalog schema; the accepted table and the plant/day metric are served through a SQL warehouse to the existing BI tool; quarantine and unresolved rows are queryable by quality; lineage and audit come from the catalog. Strengths: one home for the contract, retained history by design, governed access, room for the other plants and the assistant. Costs: a new operating surface, AWS identity and network work Noor has not approved, dual operation during coexistence, and platform usage the $1,500 ceiling does not authorize.

Path B, strengthen the existing path: keep SQL Server and the nightly package, make the extract idempotent by delivery, stage corrections under the same revision rule, compute the contract metric in a versioned view, publish a snapshot table with `evidence_as_of` and a stale flag, and point the board at it. Strengths: no new platform, the DBA owns the estate, the burden fits Leo's hours. Costs: hand-built retention and quarantine, the package's failure modes remain, the DBA's Tuesday and Thursday windows become the critical path, and nothing is gained for sensor data or documents.

I provisionally prefer Path A for a one-plant scheduled pilot because the contract, retention and stale labelling are the product, not add-ons, and the daily decision does not need streaming. That choice reverses if Noor cannot approve a path within the pilot window, if the DBA denies extraction, or if the baseline shows the disagreement comes mostly from the plant sheet, which either path fixes by policy. Path B is what I would recommend if operating budget is the binding constraint, and it is the coexistence path during migration either way.

### 7. Governed boundaries on AWS
Draw the chosen compute model accurately: classic compute in Cinderline's AWS account, or serverless compute in a Databricks-managed plane, each with separately verified identity and network access to the bucket and to any SQL Server path. No pattern is approved here. Identities: a pipeline service principal with read on the landing bucket and write on the raw, quarantine and accepted schemas; an analyst group with read on the metric view only; a quality group with read on quarantine and unresolved; the operator with run and repair rights and no table ownership. Noor classifies real fields before any real delivery; synthetic data runs first. Test permitted and denied actions with representative identities; administrator success proves nothing about least privilege.

### 8. Migration, reconciliation and rollback
Wave 0 agrees the contract, admission rules, access, environment, operator and limits. Wave 1 runs the pilot path in parallel with the current report on one plant, the same population and business days, for five staffed days. Reconciliation compares, per plant and day: distinct inspection keys; accepted counts; inspected and defective totals; every known correction and its revision; duplicates by delivery; quarantined rows and reasons; missing keys; and the snapshot identity a reader saw. Matching totals alone are insufficient; the North day matches at 20/1 only if A resolves to v2 and B is disclosed.

Cutover conditions, proposed not observed: five agreed days meeting the criteria, sign-off on meaning and access, one alert and replay rehearsal inside a Tuesday or Thursday window, and a named operator who has run the runbook once. The data lead and operations owner switch the read path; the old package keeps running through an agreed window. Rollback is a read-path change: restore the prior board, record which snapshot users saw, keep raw evidence, coordinate corrections with quality. No operational write authority moves.

### 9. Demo and presentation sequence
The sequence for the readout meeting, forty minutes: (1) the disputed day, three numbers on one slide, no blame; (2) the five rows and the accepted state, 20/1; (3) the same file delivered again, unchanged; (4) the approved correction, 22/1 once; (5) back on the 20/1 baseline, a re-typed row at the same revision: blocked, the 20/1 snapshot marked stale with the reason; (6) the night replayed under the contract, showing what the board would have said at 07:30; (7) the two paths on one comparison table; (8) the charter and the decision being asked for. Each step ends with an explain-back question; the key one, after step 5: "Does an explicitly stale board beat a silently wrong one for your meeting, and who acts on the reason?"

Opening line: "We will follow one synthetic correction into the agreed defect rate. This shows what the pilot should test; it does not prove real source connectivity or production performance." If a live step fails, say so, show the labelled prepared table, keep execution unverified, and return actual output or a precise blocker at the agreed update. Never present the prepared table as a live run.

### 10. Proof-of-value charter
Hypothesis: the approved one-plant population can be interpreted consistently, served before 07:30 with an honest freshness statement, and operated within the disclosed hours. Baseline first, on the same population: source-to-board timing, duplicate and correction counts, reconciliation hours by role, and how many mornings the board was partial or stale.

Scope: one plant, agreed fields, five staffed days, the existing board as the consumer, and synthetic cases for exact replay, late older revision, approved later revision, equal-revision conflict, invalid quantity, incomplete delivery, failure after raw retention and failure after publication. Proposed criteria: exact reconciliation except named accepted exceptions; valid business days for the whole population; every delivery published within 60 minutes of arrival, a miss failing the criterion unless the acceptor waived its cause before the test, and every morning board carrying a truthful freshness label; replay leaves accepted totals unchanged; a conflict blocks and labels; the operator demonstrates alert receipt at 06:30 and a replay inside the pilot's hours. Stop conditions: unapproved data or access, spending beyond actual authorization, a measurement basis changed mid-test, a material scope change. Readout per criterion: target, observed, population and window, input and configuration version, evidence reference, exceptions, status, owner, next action; incurred usage reported apart from projections.

Capacity, against Leo's disclosed hours: two engineers at about four hours a week each for eight weeks is 64 engineer-hours. This is a proposed plan, not an observation; reconciliation hours for the baseline are logged by the people who spend them, not by the engineers.

| Weeks | Work | Engineer-hours | Who | Window |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Wave 0: contract, admission and completeness rules agreed; access requests; synthetic environment; baseline timing and duplicate counts from existing logs; runbook draft | 16 | both engineers, with Imani and Dev | daytime; any database change in Dev's Tuesday or Thursday window |
| 3–4 | Pipeline over the eight synthetic cases; alert routed to the 06:30 check; conflict-withdrawal step written with quality | 16 | both engineers | daytime |
| 5 | Alert and replay rehearsal; the operator runs the runbook once | 8 | one engineer and the operator | one Tuesday or Thursday evening |
| 6 | Five staffed parallel days: the 06:30 check and the daily reconciliation, about 1.5 hours a day | 8 | the operator and one engineer | 06:00–18:00 only |
| 7–8 | Readout evidence, the forty-minute sequence, cleanup | 16 | both engineers | daytime |

That uses all 64 hours. If a week runs over, drop in this order: presentation polish beyond one dry run; any synthetic case beyond the eight named; a working Path B prototype (compare on paper instead). Never dropped: the stale label, the conflict block, the reconciliation and the rehearsal; if those do not fit, the pilot slips a week rather than shrinks. The five staffed days are scheduled outside the analyst's absence week, because the parallel run is compared against the analyst's workbook; if the calendar forces an overlap, Sam names a stand-in who has walked the workbook once before day 1. After week 8 the hours fall, so the handoff leaves the operator only the 06:30 check (about fifteen minutes a day) and replay on demand; anything more waits for Elena's decision.

### 11. Value model
All inputs are hypothetical and labelled. Gross annual labour value is hours/week × 48 × $60; year-one cost is $12,000 recurring plus $15,000 implementation, $27,000.

| Scenario | Hours/week | Gross value | Year-one net |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 5 | $14,400 | -$12,600 |
| Base | 10 | $28,800 | $1,800 |
| High | 15 | $43,200 | $16,200 |

Break-even is 27,000 / 2,880 = 9.375 hours/week; the base recurring-year net is $16,800 before omitted costs. Priya's hypothetical planning figure is about thirteen hours a week, to be measured in the baseline, so the high case exceeds it; capped at 13 hours it yields $37,440 gross and $10,440 year-one net, and anything above that needs a different, measured benefit. Released time is redeployed capacity, not cash, unless the customer decides otherwise. Avoided misdirected investigations are a separate line at $0 in the base case until the incident log supplies a count; at one prevented event a month the hypothetical arithmetic is 12 × (4 × $60 + 9 × $250) = $29,880, which is why it is measured and not promised. Excluded: internal operations time, training, storage and networking, migration delay, dual operation, and the DBA's change-window cost. Real prices need current product, cloud, region and commercial terms.

### 12. Alternatives and the objection
Three alternatives are compared on correctness, morning availability, stale labelling, recovery, operating effort and complete cost: Path A, Path B, and adopting the contract in the workbook alone. The third removes the mean-of-rates error and the negative adjustment tomorrow at zero platform cost; it is the honest floor every other option must beat. If Leo says "we already have a warehouse and cannot run another platform," the answer is: "That burden is real. Path B keeps your estate under the same contract; the question is whether hand-built retention and quarantine fit the DBA's windows. Let us measure that in the parallel run before recommending either."

### 13. A mixed outcome, read out honestly
Suppose the five days produce this: reconciliation exact on four days and off by one duplicate on the fifth because a manual rerun bypassed delivery labelling; 60-minute publication met for four of five deliveries, the miss caused by a Thursday change window nobody had waived; one equal-revision conflict blocked as designed, but quality took three days to withdraw the re-typed row because no one owned that step; the DBA denied CDC, so extraction ran from the nightly export; Noor approved synthetic data only. The readout, in the charter's statuses: correctness fail on one day of five, cause named, fix in admission; availability fail on one delivery of five, scheduling cause named; conflict handling passed technically and failed operationally; real-data criteria not tested. The recommendation is neither expansion nor abandonment: adopt the contract and the stale label on Path B now, assign the conflict-withdrawal owner, retest the two failed criteria on three more days, and decide on Path A only after Noor's review. A pilot that returns this is doing its job.

### 14. Handoff
Subject: Cinderline quality pilot — decisions and next evidence

Thank you for the disclosures, including the inventory, the metric as computed today, the night of 2 March and the capacity limits. Our proposed first scope is one plant and the unit-based plant/day defect rate under the attached metric contract; the maintenance assistant stays separate. The synthetic five-row walk explains expected behaviour; it does not validate real connectivity, network configuration or production performance.

Imani and Mara: confirm the business-day boundary, restatement rule and stale-label wording. Sam: confirm the three figures for 2 March and retire the mean-of-rates cell once the contract view exists. Dev and Leo: confirm ERP version and topology, extraction permission, delivery labelling on rerun, whether the package can write a completion marker per run or per plant, and the baseline plan. Noor: own classification and the AWS path review. Leo: nominate the operator and the conflict-withdrawal owner. Priya: confirm baseline hours and start the incident count.

I propose reviewing these outputs on a fictional date two weeks out, to be confirmed. That review should finalize the charter, revise the design, or retain the current path while closing a named blocker. Elena approves any real scope and spending; the value model is not a savings promise. Open risks: DBA availability, the unapproved network path, the plant sheet's informal authority, and the absence of a wrong-decision log. Please correct any assumption before we treat it as agreed.

### Technical appendix
Accepted-state walk for North, 2 March: after deliveries D1 and D2, raw 5, accepted A v2 12/1 and C v1 8/0 prepared, quarantine B, publication held because D1's package run did not complete; after D3, which completes the run and carries the late re-export, raw 6, accepted unchanged, snapshot 20/1 at 5.0% with `evidence_as_of` 11:15; after approved A v3, raw 7, accepted A v3 14/1 and C, snapshot 22/1 at 4.5%, one effect; after exact replay, raw 8, unchanged, no second effect; conflict branch applied to the 20/1 baseline in a fresh simulation: raw 6, A unresolved, only C 8/0 prepared and that is not a report, publication blocked, snapshot 20/1 stale with reason; a later A v3 does not clear a conflict retained in history.

Snapshot fields: `plant`, `business_day`, `inspected_units`, `defective_units`, `defect_rate`, `accepted_inspections`, `quarantined_inspections`, `unresolved_keys`, `evidence_as_of`, `snapshot_id`, `publication_status`, `stale_reason`.

Runbook: alert to the operator's 06:30 check, not a mailbox; replay from retained raw with delivery labels; conflict withdrawal owned by quality with a recorded decision; rollback by read-path switch; cleanup only after acceptance.

### Recommendation
Resolve the named discovery and access gaps, adopt the metric contract and stale labelling regardless of platform, and review a bounded charter. Do not declare production readiness or commit to expansion. Prefer the smallest path that meets the accepted decision and the disclosed capacity, even if that means Path B first.
scenarios.reasoning: This submission keeps the same decision, denominator, correction rule and evidence boundaries throughout, and now carries one policy from the five-row example to the operator's runbook: accepted A v2 and C v1 at 20/1, replay unchanged, an older revision refused, a valid A v3 giving 22/1 once, a conflicting delivery blocking publication while the last verified snapshot stays visible and explicitly stale. It reads the failure timeline as the difference between explicitly stale and silently wrong, proposes two defensible paths including one that keeps the customer's existing estate, fits the work to the disclosed 64 engineer-hours and says what is dropped first, and shows a mixed outcome that still yields a decision. Its security path is conditional rather than invented; its migration is reversible; its demo has an honest fallback; its pilot can produce a negative decision; and its value calculation exposes sensitivity and keeps an unmeasured avoided-cost line out of the base case. The self-assessment below is educational reflection. It is not independent expert review, official onboarding acceptance, a credential, or a measure of employer-level readiness.

rubric.weak: Assumes requirements, stakeholders, and benefits from the initial request.
rubric.partial: Identifies some gaps but misses decision timing, access, or acceptors.
rubric.strong: Maps the buying decision, stakeholders, facts, missing inputs, assumptions, and questions that can change the design.

rubric.weak: Confuses source authority, compute boundaries, metrics, or correction semantics.
rubric.partial: A plausible path has one or more material unexamined boundaries.
rubric.strong: Explains source/raw/accepted/serving responsibilities, key/revision rules, AWS identity/network boundaries, and operating limits accurately.

rubric.weak: Presents one inevitable target with no credible fallback.
rubric.partial: Mentions alternatives but does not compare consequences or rollback.
rubric.strong: Compares a meaningful current-state alternative, justifies the provisional choice, and defines reversible migration and reconsideration conditions.

rubric.weak: Uses jargon or hides failed/uncertain behavior.
rubric.partial: Gives a coherent story but lacks explain-back or a transparent fallback.
rubric.strong: Adapts the narrative to the audience, exposes evidence, handles failure honestly, and writes a usable owned handoff.

rubric.weak: Treats targets, examples, or clicks as observed success.
rubric.partial: Has some thresholds but weak baseline, population, recovery, or readout.
rubric.strong: Defines comparable baseline, scoped tests, exact expected outputs, acceptance owners, evidence states, and a decision-ready readout.

rubric.weak: Claims guaranteed savings, compliance, or production readiness.
rubric.partial: Labels assumptions but omits sensitivity, exclusions, or unresolved authority.
rubric.strong: Shows reproducible hypothetical arithmetic, sensitivity and realization limits, source/availability caveats, and the next evidence needed before commitment.

rubric.weak: Takes the workbook's or plant sheet's number as the metric and treats the ETL copy as a source.
rubric.partial: Names the flaw in the current metric but leaves grain, denominator, business-day boundary, restatement or exclusion disclosure unspecified.
rubric.strong: Separates systems of record from derived copies, names the approved revision signal, and writes a testable contract whose worked figures reconcile the disputed day.

rubric.weak: Deduplicates by row or arrival order, lets a later delivery overwrite, or averages away conflicts.
rubric.partial: Handles duplicates and corrections but not conflicting deliveries, the explicitly stale snapshot, or a named failure boundary.
rubric.strong: Applies the preserved policy end to end: retained raw evidence, replay-safe totals, older revisions refused, conflicts blocking with the last verified snapshot visibly stale, and recovery per boundary.

rubric.weak: Assumes continuous support, overnight response or an unnamed operator.
rubric.partial: Names an operator but does not fit alerts, replay, change windows and approvals to the disclosed hours.
rubric.strong: Designs alert routing, replay, conflict withdrawal and cutover inside the disclosed capacity and says what is dropped if it is exceeded.

rubric.weak: Treats the latest number on the board as current and the failure night as an isolated IT problem.
rubric.partial: Notes staleness but does not connect it to the meeting's action, or presents avoided cost as measured.
rubric.strong: Shows how an explicitly stale, dated snapshot changes the decision, separates facts from hypotheses in the timeline, and keeps unmeasured avoided cost out of the base case.

scenarios.title: Northbrook Holdings: enterprise coexistence and modernization
scenarios.context:
Northbrook Holdings is an original fictional industrial group that makes pressed and machined components at two plants, Ashcombe and Corvane. Eight months ago it acquired Vale Components, a fictional supplier with plants at Fennick and Marrow Point. A third business unit, Tessaly Rail Systems, builds signalling equipment under a fictional regulator whose rules restrict where its maintenance and telemetry data may be held.

The three estates do not look alike. Northbrook runs an on-premises enterprise warehouse (a fictional appliance called Granite: 18 TB, about 640 nightly jobs) that feeds a group BI service on Azure with forty certified dashboards and roughly three hundred users, plus a monthly finance close pack built from spreadsheet macros. Vale runs a lakehouse workspace on AWS with its own account, its own identity provider, its own Unity Catalog metastore and its own governed sharing to three external suppliers. Tessaly keeps its restricted records in an on-premises hall in the fictional Nordland jurisdiction and a small Google Cloud project in an in-jurisdiction region for a telemetry archive.

The group CIO has circulated a one-page memo titled "One platform by year end". It asks for "everything on one analytics platform, on one cloud, by the end of fiscal Q3", and names you, the field engineer coordinating the proposed engagement, as the person who will "bring the plan". The memo also says the Ashcombe plant-floor dashboard, Line Pulse, must become "real time", and that the group should "stop paying for two of everything".

What the memo does not say is most of what you need. ### Capstone guide

Northbrook Holdings, a fictional industrial group, has acquired Vale
Components and inherited three estates on three clouds, one of them under a
data-residency rule. The CIO's memo asks for one platform by year end. This
capstone asks you to find out what the evidence actually supports, and to say
so to two audiences. Open it at `#/practice/dbxfe-capstone-coexistence`; the
data pack lives under `content/exercises/capstone-coexistence/`.

Everything in the engagement is fictional or hypothetical. No workspace,
cloud account, paid service or model call is needed, and none is executed.

#### What makes this one different

The first capstone (Cinderline) builds one bounded pilot from a first
conversation. The second builds a service-knowledge assistant with controlled
actions. This one starts with an answer already assumed by executives and
tests it against contracts, dependencies, security boundaries, residency,
latency, a blackout and a budget ceiling. The best submission is not a
migration plan for everything; it is a segmented decision in which some
workloads stay, some coexist through governed sharing, some migrate in waves,
and some are deliberately not migrated yet, with a dated condition for
reconsidering each.

#### Stages

1. **Read the brief and open the disclosures deliberately.** The brief is
   missing most of what you need on purpose. Each of the eight stakeholder
   disclosures changes something: a contract date, an undocumented
   dependency, a security condition, a residency rule that covers metadata, a
   budget ceiling, a BI team's parity rule, the real latency need, and what the
   CIO would accept. Record what each one changed and what is still unknown.
2. **Segment the workloads.** Place all 26 inventory rows using
   `workload-segmentation.md`. Name the driver for each placement and the
   evidence it needs. Add the disclosed dependencies to `dependencies.csv`
   marked as disclosed.
3. **Fill the three-cloud matrix honestly.** Every cell starts as
   "unknown — needs verification". Source what you can from each cloud's own
   current documentation; leave the rest marked and turn them into open
   questions with owners. A cell filled from memory is still unknown.
4. **Decide sharing or federation versus movement** for the four cross-estate
   datasets, each with recipient, revocation, freshness, cost and failure
   behaviour.
5. **Design security and operations:** three identity boundaries, the
   security objection met without cross-estate group membership, a residency
   control that covers metadata, audit evidence, owners and runbook entries.
6. **Reconcile.** The two totals files disagree. Find both causes, state the
   corrected totals, and define the parallel-run gate before you read the
   worked answer.
7. **Plan wave 1's cutover and rollback** inside the quarter, around the
   blackout and the notice date, with a rehearsal and a rollback owner.
8. **Complete the cost worksheet** as a range against the ceiling, with
   currency, period, units and exclusions, and no real prices or savings
   claims.
9. **Write both readouts and the decision record** from the templates, with a
   concise presentation sequence and a section on what the evidence does not
   justify.
10. **Reveal the model and self-assess** against the seven rubric dimensions.
    A different path is not wrong if its unknowns and conditions are as
    explicit.

#### Supporting modules

- [Architecture reasoning and migration decisions](#/module/dbxfe-m08): two

  migration, reconciliation and rollback.
- [Warehouse and distributed-platform migrations](#/module/dbxfe-warehouse-migration):

- [Sharing, federation and interoperability](#/module/dbxfe-sharing):

- [AWS](#/module/dbxfe-aws), [Azure](#/module/dbxfe-azure) and

- [Unity Catalog and governance responsibilities](#/module/dbxfe-m06) and

- [Compute choices, cost and FinOps reasoning](#/module/dbxfe-finops): the

- [Business intelligence and semantic delivery](#/module/dbxfe-bi): what the

- [Production operations, observability and recovery](#/module/dbxfe-operations):

- [Discovery and qualification](#/module/dbxfe-m02),
  [Competition, coexistence and business value](#/module/dbxfe-m11) and

#### Supporting labs and field guides

#### How the pack is used

`inventory.csv` and `dependencies.csv` are the facts you start from and are

### 1. Discovery: what the memo assumes and what the disclosures changed
The memo asks for one platform, one cloud, everything, by 31 December, with Line Pulse "real time". Those are four assumptions and one undefined word; the disclosures replaced most of them with facts.

Dana's contract dates make the calendar the first constraint: Granite's support renews on 1 April with ninety days' notice, so the renew-or-give-notice decision falls on 31 December, inside the blackout, and notice would fix a hard 31 March exit for eighteen terabytes and 640 jobs. Vale's committed-use agreement has fourteen months left with undisclosed amounts: a reason not to move Vale, not a number. Kofi withdrew "real time": supervisors act on a stoppage within five minutes, and the current fifteen-minute refresh misses the shift change. Katja named the dependency nobody wrote down: the Vale demand forecast reads the group price list in Granite over a database link and fails silently to last week's prices; Line Pulse joins to a hand-maintained shift calendar. Mateus's objection is a design input: no Northbrook directory groups in Vale's catalogs, no shared storage credentials across clouds, recipient-scoped and revocable exchange only, and no Northbrook compute in Vale's account until Vale has assessed Northbrook's on-premises network. Ingrid's rule is the one I could not have guessed: for Tessaly, the metadata of restricted datasets is itself restricted, no hyperscaler region is approved for an analytics platform or its metadata (the archive's in-jurisdiction region was approved for storage only), and approval takes about two quarters. Beatrix's ceiling is a hypothetical USD 450,000 for the quarter, not an authorization. Rosalind will accept a dashboard being re-pointed only after side-by-side parity on the same period. Helena will accept two platforms for a while given the date it becomes one or the reason it never will.

Still unknown, with owners: whether either identity provider can federate to the other estate's platform (Mateus and the Northbrook identity lead); whether any managed service on any cloud can hold Tessaly's metadata in-jurisdiction (Ingrid, from primary documentation and the regulator); which of the 640 jobs have any reader (the Northbrook data lead, from Granite's query logs); the measured Line Pulse latency baseline (Kofi); real prices, Vale's committed amounts and whether a shorter Granite extension exists (Dana); who at Northbrook consumes Vale's supplier-quality summary, and how often (Vale's quality lead with Northbrook procurement). Each sits in the decision record beside the decision it blocks.

### 2. Two defensible paths, and the disposition the memo forgot
**Path A: extend Vale's estate into the group platform.** Vale's AWS account, metastore and operating team become the group's primary analytics platform; Northbrook workloads migrate to it in waves; the Azure BI service reads it across clouds; Tessaly stays put. Its strengths are real: proven governance and operations, a team that runs pipelines daily, and a committed-use agreement that argues for adding load there. Its costs are the ones Mateus and Rosalind named: Northbrook identities would need federation into Vale's account or a second identity plane; every Northbrook dashboard would read across a cloud boundary with egress and latency nobody has measured; and two organisations' data would share one metastore before a separation-of-duties model exists. On the facts in the pack, A is defensible after four conditions are met, and not before: identity federation answered (matrix row 1); a separation-of-duties model for one shared metastore; a measured cross-cloud BI read path (row 11); and Vale's assessment of Northbrook's on-premises network, without which Mateus allows no Northbrook compute in Vale's account.

**Path B: two governed estates that share, and one that stays.** Northbrook stands up its own lakehouse workspace on Azure beside its BI service and landing storage; Vale keeps its AWS estate; the cross-estate datasets move through governed sharing rather than copies or database links; Tessaly's restricted data stays on-premises with an approval track opened now. Its strengths: the BI service keeps a same-cloud read path, Vale's boundary is preserved, and the identity question becomes "can Northbrook's own directory reach Northbrook's own workspace". Its costs: two platforms to operate, two metastores, sharing freshness and cost still unmeasured, and a Northbrook team learning a platform it has not run. Under either path, "stop paying for two of everything" does not happen this quarter; the Granite decision is a notice date, not a switch-off.

The two paths on the same eight criteria (the technical readout adds the evidence for each cell):

| Criterion | Path A: extend Vale's estate | Path B: two estates that share |
|---|---|---|
| Identity and trust boundaries | Northbrook identities federated into Vale's account or a second identity plane; federation unknown (row 1); Mateus refuses Northbrook groups in Vale's catalogs | Three directories stay three; access across estates by share recipient only |
| Residency (data and metadata) | Tessaly stays out; no difference | Tessaly stays out; no difference |
| BI continuity | Every Beacon dashboard reads across a cloud boundary; latency unmeasured (row 11) | Same-cloud read path; dashboards re-pointed one at a time after parity |
| Latency for the plant floor | Line Pulse not moved this quarter | Line Pulse not moved this quarter |
| Contract and blackout fit | Adds load under Vale's committed-use agreement (amounts undisclosed); Granite notice and blackout apply as in B | Granite notice and blackout apply; Vale's commitment untouched |
| Operations (owners, runbooks) | One proven team runs more; separation of duties across two organisations undefined | Two platforms and two teams; Northbrook learns a platform it has not run |
| Cost range | Unknown: the worksheet prices Path B only, and federation and cross-cloud reads are unsized | 282,500 / 375,000 / 513,000 USD, hypothetical (§9) |
| Reversibility | Harder: two organisations' data in one metastore before separation of duties exists | Read path only; revert by re-pointing (§8) |

**Not yet.** Three workloads get the disposition the memo forgot, each with an owner and a dated condition. *Line Pulse* does not move in Q3. Its requirement was defined this week, its feed and the shift calendar are on-premises, and moving a plant-floor screen through a blackout to meet an unmeasured latency target is how a plant loses a screen it trusts. Condition: the Ashcombe plant IT lead measures the end-to-end delay for two weeks without changing the screen, by Friday 27 November; after the blackout, a prototype outside the screen must show a stoppage within five minutes on a normal shift; Kofi decides at the wave-2 gate on Friday 29 January whether Line Pulse enters wave 2 or waits another quarter. *The finance close pack and the twelve finance dashboards* stay on Granite through the year-end close; the group financial controller and Rosalind decide at the same 29 January gate whether they enter wave 2's parallel run, with Rosalind's parity rule as the test. *Tessaly's restricted records* stay until Ingrid's regulator answers a specific written question; Ingrid sends it in weeks 1–2, and at about two quarters the answer is expected around mid-2027, not before.

My provisional recommendation is Path B for the fiscal quarter, scoped to one wave, with the A-versus-B consolidation question decided at a dated gate after the wave has run. Not because two platforms are better: because the evidence supports a first wave and coexistence, and does not yet support consolidating Vale, moving Tessaly, or moving finance and the plant floor.

Tessaly: no compute is proposed, and whether serverless processing can leave a region (row 3) is one reason none will be until the regulator answers. ### 7. Reconciliation
The pack's two total files disagree, and the naive comparison lies twice. Summing the source quantity column while ignoring the unit gives 89,435 against a target of 90,685: a difference of 1,250 that looks like one clean cause. It is not, because the source rows are in mixed units. Fennick reports 9,940 *cases*, and Vale's packaging master says a case is twelve units, so the source in units is 48,320 + 31,175 + 119,280 = 198,775. The target carries 49,570 + 31,175 + 9,940 = 90,685 for two reasons: its extract was cut on 2 September, before revision R-2026-08-117 reversed 1,250 units at Ashcombe on 3 September, and its loader took Fennick's number as units. The corrected consolidated totals are Ashcombe 48,320, Corvane 31,175, Fennick 119,280, group 198,775 units. The value column confirms the diagnosis: values match except at Ashcombe, where the target is 62,500.00 higher (1,250 units at 50.00), because value came from invoices and is untouched by the case mistake.

The parallel-run reconciliation gate therefore has four parts: units declared per row and converted once at a stated conversion; an as-of timestamp on every total, with late revisions listed by identifier; key-level comparison per plant and period, never a group total; and named accepted exceptions with an owner. A matching group total is not a pass.

### 8. Cutover and rollback for wave 1
The quarter is 1 October to 31 December; the group-wide change blackout runs 8 December to 2 January (the brief); the notice decision is 31 December. So wave 1 must be cut over by Friday 4 December, and the finance workloads are out of it by construction. Weeks 1–2: agree the price-list contract and the dashboard parity method with Rosalind, schedule the network review, request Granite's query logs, send the regulator question. Weeks 3–5: build the workspace, land the price list and the dimensions, open the share to Vale, run the first parallel comparison. Week 6: rehearse rollback as an executed sequence with expected outputs, before anything a reader sees is re-pointed. Weeks 7–9: parallel run over three complete weekly cycles, including the Sunday forecasts of 15, 22 and 29 November; re-point dashboards one at a time, each after parity. Week 10, by Friday 4 December: cutover, meaning the last dashboard re-pointed and the forecast's database link revoked (not deleted). Nothing changes from 8 December. Recovery window to 31 January, through the blackout, with Granite still loading.

Triggers for pause or revert: a key-level reconciliation failure not on the exceptions list; a dashboard failing parity after re-pointing; a stale share on a forecast night; an unfinished network review at the rehearsal. The rollback owner re-points affected dashboards to the Azure reporting database, restores the forecast's database link, records which users saw which source, and deletes nothing. Only the read path moves; no write authority changes in wave 1.

Communication: the BI lead tells Beacon's roughly three hundred users which dashboards move and when, a week before each re-point and again on the day; Katja tells Vale planning before the first Sunday the forecast reads the share; Kofi tells his supervisors that Line Pulse does not change this quarter; the rollback owner announces any revert the same day, naming which source each dashboard showed and when.

The 31 December notice decision is taken on the wave's evidence, not on the memo: give notice with a 31 March exit only if wave 1 reconciled and every Granite producer and consumer has a dated destination by 31 March, including Line Pulse, the MES staging feeds, the ERP, CRM and HR extracts, the Tessaly totals load, the finance close pack and the Conduit jobs not yet placed; otherwise renew for the shortest term the vendor offers, a question for Dana now. On this plan Line Pulse and finance are decided on 29 January, so the expected answer on 31 December is the shortest renewal.

### 9. Commercial sensitivity
All numbers are the worksheet's hypothetical inputs in USD for fiscal Q3 (1 October to 31 December). No real price, discount or savings claim is made. For Path B wave 1 plus coexistence, low / base / high: platform usage 60,000 / 95,000 / 150,000; storage 1,500 / 3,000 / 6,000; data movement 2,000 / 6,000 / 15,000; dual running of Granite support at the quarter's share, 120,000 in every case, unavoidable given the notice date; partner migration labour at a hypothetical 1,400 per day for 60 / 90 / 130 days, 84,000 / 126,000 / 182,000; operations and training 15,000 / 25,000 / 40,000. Totals: low 282,500, base 375,000, high 513,000 against the 450,000 ceiling. The base case fits with 75,000 headroom; the high case does not. No single input moves the total past the ceiling: from the base case, partner days alone at their high value give 431,000 and platform usage alone at its high value 430,000, both under. It takes the two of them high together (486,000), or either of them high with data movement and operations also high (454,000 or 455,000). Partner days and platform usage are the two large swings (+56,000 and +55,000), and both scale with wave-1 scope, so the control is the scope of wave 1, not the platform. Path A is not priced: the worksheet has no scenario for it, and its federation work and cross-cloud reads are unsized, so its cost range is unknown rather than lower. The "everything in Q3" line the memo implies cannot be scheduled through the blackout at all; the worksheet shows it as a base case of 1,120,000, labelled as a number for an impossible plan. Not migrating Line Pulse and finance yet costs nothing incremental this quarter, because Granite's quarter is already paid; its real cost is the renewal term chosen on 31 December, which is why that decision is made on evidence. Excluded: the BI licence, contingency, internal salaries, network circuits, tax, Tessaly's regulator process and any committed-use effect at Vale.

### 10. Executive readout and presentation sequence
The one page says, in order: the decision asked and the answer (a first wave and governed coexistence now, consolidation decided at a dated gate); what stays, coexists, moves and waits, as four short lists; the two dates that matter, 4 December and 31 December; the money as a range against the ceiling with the inputs that move it; the three risks that could reverse it; and four asks: an identity-federation answer, a network review date, the regulator question sent, and renewal term options.

The presentation sequence is eight minutes: the memo's assumption and the four facts that changed it; the segmentation picture; the price list as the wave-1 story, the undocumented link being the reason it goes first; the reconciliation example as the reason totals are not gates; the calendar; the money; the negative findings; the asks. "Why not one platform" is answered with the date the question is decided and the evidence that decides it.

### 11. Technical appendix
The technical readout carries the inventory with every disposition and driver; the dependency map with the two undocumented edges added and marked as disclosed, not documented; the matrix with the provenance of every cell; the four sharing designs with recipient, revocation, freshness, cost and failure behaviour; the trust-boundary diagram with three directories and no cross-estate group membership; the reconciliation arithmetic and gate; the wave-1 calendar, rehearsal script and rollback sequence with expected outputs; the worksheet with its formulas; and the decision record. Every platform capability it relies on is marked sourced, customer-stated or unknown; the unknown cells open the questions list, each with an owner and the decision it blocks.

### 12. What the evidence does not justify
It does not justify consolidating Vale onto a Northbrook platform, or Northbrook onto Vale's, this quarter: the identity and separation-of-duties questions are open, Vale has not assessed Northbrook's network, and the committed-use agreement is undisclosed. It does not justify moving Tessaly's data, or registering its metadata, anywhere until the regulator answers. It does not justify a "real time" Line Pulse: the requirement is five minutes and nobody has measured the current path. It does not justify giving notice on Granite to force the pace; a hard March exit with finance unmigrated is a risk to the close, not a plan. It does not justify a savings claim of any size: the worksheet has no real prices, and dual running is a cost under every option.

The recommendation reverses if identity federation proves straightforward and Mateus's conditions, including Vale's assessment of Northbrook's network, can be met inside one account (Path A becomes the consolidation route); if wave-1 reconciliation fails twice on the same cause (the wave pauses and the price-list contract is reworked); or if the regulator approves a region sooner than expected (Tessaly's archive becomes a candidate).

### Recommendation
Run wave 1 under Path B inside the quarter; replace the undocumented link with a governed share; keep finance, Line Pulse and Tessaly where they are, each with a dated reconsideration condition; take the Granite notice decision on the wave's evidence; and put the one-platform question on the steering group's agenda for the quarter after next with Path A's four conditions answered. Prefer the smallest wave that retires a real risk over the largest the calendar could hold.

scenarios.title: Harrowgate Field Services: service knowledge and controlled actions
scenarios.context:
Harrowgate Field Services is an original fictional industrial-equipment service organisation. Its technicians maintain compressors, pumps, belt drives and chillers at customer sites across three service regions (north, south, coastal). Procedures live in a versioned document library on a shared drive: some versions are superseded but still there, some documents contradict each other, and some apply to one region or one technician level only. Work is tracked in a ticketing system called the Ticket Desk, and parts are requested through a separate Parts Requisition system. The service director has asked for "an assistant that finds the right procedure for a technician and, when it works, files the parts order from the same screen."

The first conversation established this much: the library exists, technicians find procedures with plain file search, "a few" wrong-version incidents have happened, there is money in this year's tools line for a build, and the director wants a demo within the month. It did not establish how many documents or technicians there are, who owns the library and decides what is current, how access restrictions are recorded and where, what the Ticket Desk and the parts system expose to an integration, who approves a parts order and on what evidence, what a correct answer means to a technician, whether the safety lead has a view, or who would operate the assistant after the demo. Several of these are answered only in the stakeholder disclosures; some are not answered at all, and your submission should say which.

You are the field engineer proposing the engagement. The platform concepts taught in the F track — governed documents and metadata, retrieval over indexed content, evaluation and tracing, tool authorization, application state — are the educational vocabulary. No Databricks workspace, model endpoint or language model is executed by this exercise, and any product name in your design must be verified against current documentation before it appears in a real proposal. All people, documents, systems, dates, values and money in this scenario are fictional or hypothetical; no real customer, vendor or employer is described.

**What you receive** (the data pack under `content/exercises/capstone-service-knowledge/`, every file fictional and labelled so):

- `documents/` — twelve short document excerpts, each opening with header lines for id, title, version, effective date, supersedes and superseded-by, status, region and audience. A current manual and a field bulletin disagree for a subset of units; a superseded isolation procedure sits beside the current one; one supplement is region-restricted and one section is level-restricted; a draft, an unofficial wiki tip and an irrelevant administrative document are mixed in.
- `stale-content.md` — the superseded torque procedure behind a fictional incident, still the most-linked file on the drive.
- `injection-fixture.md` — a benign synthetic ticket note that "instructs" the assistant to order parts and close the ticket, with an authored answer key.
- `questions.json` — 22 labelled questions: asker role and region, whether the asker is authorized, expected source ids, sources that must not be cited, the expected answer property, category and difficulty, plus the list of blocking failures.
- `authorization-matrix.csv` — 46 rows of principal, document or action, allowed, reason.
- `templates/` — discovery synthesis, evaluation plan, authorization boundary and recommendation.

Open the disclosures deliberately, then write a complete submission before revealing the model. Several designs can be defensible if their assumptions, evidence and refusals are explicit. A refusal that names the missing approval is a correct outcome in this scenario, not a gap in the assistant.

### Capstone guide

This page is how to work the second capstone, *Service knowledge and controlled actions*, in stages. The scenario itself — the brief, the stakeholder disclosures, the nine requirements, the model submission, its reasoning and the six-dimension rubric — is at [#/practice/dbxfe-capstone-service-knowledge](#/practice/dbxfe-capstone-service-knowledge). Everything in it is fictional: Harrowgate Field Services, its regions, technicians, equipment, documents, policies, incident and money are synthetic teaching material. No Databricks workspace, endpoint or language model is executed by the capstone, and nothing you write here is a credential or a readiness judgement; the rubric is for your own reflection.

#### What the capstone asks

A fictional service organisation wants an assistant that finds the right maintenance procedure for a technician and, eventually, files parts orders. Its library holds superseded versions beside current ones, a bulletin that overrides one section of a manual for some units, a region-restricted supplement, a level-restricted section, a draft, an unofficial wiki tip and administrative noise. Its parts policy forbids an assistant to submit an order. Your job is to choose between plain search, retrieval-assisted answers and tool use, design the authority, retrieval, evaluation and authorization boundaries, and recommend a next step on evidence — including saying plainly that ordering is not justified yet and what would justify it.

#### Work it in stages

**Stage 1 — Discovery.** Read the brief, notice what it leaves out, then open the disclosures one at a time and record what each one changes. [Discovery and qualification](#/module/dbxfe-m02) teaches the synthesis; [Role and customer journey](#/module/dbxfe-m01) the responsibility map. Field guides: discovery brief (fg01), stakeholder map (fg02), requirements contract (fg03). Output: `templates/discovery-synthesis.md`.

**Stage 2 — Source authority and freshness.** Read every document header in `documents/` and `stale-content.md` before any body, and write the rule that decides which document is eligible for which asker and which wins when two current ones disagree. [Document processing and retrieval engineering](#/module/dbxfe-retrieval) and Lab L20 (retrieval quality) show why the wrong chunk wins and how metadata changes that; the RAG evaluation guide (fg17) gives the shape.

**Stage 3 — Pattern choice.** Decide between plain search, retrieval-assisted answers and tool use as two defensible paths with tradeoffs and a switching condition. [GenAI, retrieval and agents](#/module/dbxfe-genai) separates finding information from taking action; [Managed AI building blocks](#/module/dbxfe-ai-platform) covers when simple retrieval beats autonomous tool selection; [Architecture and migration](#/module/dbxfe-m08) and the architecture decision guide (fg04) give the decision-record form.

**Stage 4 — Retrieval and evaluation design.** Work `questions.json` by hand first: for each question decide eligibility, winner and outcome, then compare with the expected property. Define metrics with numerators and denominators and the blocking failures. [GenAI evaluation, traces and failure analysis](#/module/dbxfe-genai-eval) and Lab L21 (evaluation traces) separate retrieval failure from reasoning failure from a denied tool. Output: `templates/evaluation-plan.md`.

**Stage 5 — Authorization and state boundary.** Use `authorization-matrix.csv` and `injection-fixture.md`. [Tools, MCP and action authorization](#/module/dbxfe-tools) and Lab L22 (tool authorization) show a system prompt is not access control and how untrusted content requesting an action is rejected under policy; the untrusted-content threat review (fg18) and tool-action review (fg19) guides structure it. [Unity Catalog and governance](#/module/dbxfe-m06) with Lab L14 and the access review guide (fg06), and [Identity, authorization and audit](#/module/dbxfe-identity), cover delegated permissions and negative tests. [Databricks Apps and application architecture](#/module/dbxfe-apps) and the application state guide (fg20) settle where each fact lives. Output: `templates/authorization-boundary.md`.

**Stage 6 — Operational ownership.** Name an owner or write "unassigned" for the library, operation, the evaluation set, access rules and the parts policy, with the incident path. [Production operations, observability and recovery](#/module/dbxfe-operations) and the escalation packet guide (fg31).

**Stage 7 — Demo sequence and technical appendix.** Ten minutes at most: a provenance-bearing answer, a version conflict, a denied action, the injection refusal, an explain-back question and a transparent fallback. [Demos that teach and prove](#/module/dbxfe-m09) with the demo script (fg24) and demo failure plan (fg25) guides.

**Stage 8 — Pilot charter, evidence and recommendation.** Write the charter with stop conditions, then the one-page recommendation with its negative-outcome section. [Proofs of value](#/module/dbxfe-m10) with the PoV charter (fg26) and evidence ledger (fg27) guides; [Competition and business value](#/module/dbxfe-m11) for the alternatives memo (fg29); [Field execution and capstone](#/module/dbxfe-m12) for the executive readout (fg30) and handoff plan (fg32). Output: `templates/recommendation.md` for the recommendation, a pilot charter in your own structure (the pack has no charter template; the PoV charter guide gives the shape), plus the appendix.

#### How the data pack is used

The pack lives at `content/exercises/capstone-service-knowledge/`; its `README.md` is the dictionary. `documents/` is the corpus and carries the planted trouble; `stale-content.md` is the superseded procedure behind the incident; `injection-fixture.md` is the benign planted instruction with its answer key; `questions.json` is the labelled set with authorized and unauthorized askers, must-not-cite sources and blocking failures; `authorization-matrix.csv` is the starting matrix that nothing enforces; `templates/` are the four submission templates. Only Markdown, JSON and CSV; nothing to install. If you run a local retrieval experiment over the files, label it as your own local execution. The pack creates nothing on your machine; delete only your working copies and keep your written answers.

#### When you are done

Reveal the model submission only after your own is complete, then read the rubric's six dimensions — discovery, technical correctness, tradeoffs, communication, measurable evidence, decision quality — as reflection prompts. Several designs are defensible when their assumptions, evidence and refusals are explicit; a refusal that names the missing approval is a correct outcome here. The third capstone, enterprise coexistence and modernization, follows this one.

A source-authority and freshness policy: how status, version, effective date, supersession, bulletin scope, region and audience decide which documents are eligible for an asker, which wins when two current documents disagree, when the assistant must ask rather than choose, and how superseded, draft and unofficial content is handled when it is explicitly requested.

An operational ownership plan naming the owner (or "unassigned") and funding status for the document library, platform operation, the evaluation set, access rules and the parts policy, with the incident path for a wrong answer, a refused action and an injection event.

A demo sequence of at most ten minutes showing a provenance-bearing answer, a version conflict, a denied action and the injection refusal, with an explain-back question and a transparent fallback, plus a technical appendix listing components, data flow, trace fields and what is mocked.
